result: The manuscript establishes the historical context and formal introduction of trained immunity. Claims C1, C5, and C6 describe the historical view that immune memory was exclusive to adaptive immunity, while C2 and C3 define trained immunity as enhanced innate immune responses following prior exposure. C4 states that the term was formally introduced in 2011.
evaluation: These claims are well-supported by citations and represent established historical and definitional knowledge. The progression from historical understanding (C1, C5, C6) to the discovery of trained immunity (C2, C3) and formal naming (C4) is logically coherent and appropriately referenced.

result: The manuscript traces key milestones in trained immunity research from 1961 to 2024. These include the discovery of SAR in plants (C7), identification of epigenetic modifications (C8), mobilization of hematopoietic progenitors (C9), antitumor effects of trained neutrophils (C10), proposal as cancer treatment strategy (C11), control of various cancers by trained macrophages (C12), and clinical trials (C13).
evaluation: All claims are supported by appropriate citations and represent a chronological summary of the field's development. The timeline is consistent with Figure 1 and provides historical context for the review. These are primarily literature review claims rather than novel findings.

result: The manuscript describes the 2016 refinement of trained immunity terminology to distinguish enhanced immunity (trained immunity) from weakened responses (tolerized innate immunity).
evaluation: Both claims are supported by citation to Netea et al., 2016 and represent an important conceptual clarification in the field. This definitional refinement is well-established and appropriately referenced.

result: The manuscript contrasts innate and adaptive immunity mechanisms. Trained innate immune cells respond via pattern recognition receptors detecting PAMPs/DAMPs (C16, C17) rather than specific antigen recognition, enabling faster secondary responses than adaptive immunity (C18).
evaluation: These claims describe fundamental immunological principles supported by appropriate citations (Medzhitov and Janeway, 2002; Iwasaki and Medzhitov, 2015). The mechanistic distinction between innate and adaptive immunity is well-established knowledge.

result: The manuscript presents 2022 global cancer statistics: nearly 20 million diagnoses and approximately 9.7 million deaths.
evaluation: Both claims are supported by citation to Bray et al., 2024 (IARC report) and provide epidemiological context for the clinical significance of cancer immunotherapy research.

result: The manuscript describes current immunotherapy efficacy: ICIs have improved survival in NSCLC and melanoma (C21), but pancreatic cancer responds poorly (C22), and even in responsive cancers, ORR remains below 40% (C23).
evaluation: Claims are supported by appropriate citations (Sharma et al., 2023; Leinwand and Miller, 2020). These establish the clinical rationale for exploring trained immunity as a complementary approach. The statistics provide important context for the field.

result: The manuscript states that HSPCs and innate immune cells undergo epigenetic, metabolic, and transcriptional reprogramming when exposed to training agents like β-glucan, BCG, or nanotherapeutics.
evaluation: This claim is supported by multiple citations covering different aspects of trained immunity mechanisms. It represents a well-established mechanistic understanding in the field and is consistent with Figure 2.

result: The manuscript describes β-glucan and BCG as central trained immunity inducers. β-glucan reprograms HSPCs to generate trained neutrophils and macrophages controlling tumors (C25). BCG exerts antitumor effects partly through trained immunity (C26) and intravenous BCG reprograms HSPCs and enhances myelopoiesis (C27).
evaluation: All claims are supported by appropriate citations (Ding et al., 2023; Kalafati et al., 2020; van Puffelen et al., 2020; Kaufmann et al., 2018). These represent established mechanisms of central trained immunity.

result: The manuscript presents conflicting findings on BCG administration routes. Intravenous BCG increases CD8+ T cells and reduces MDSCs (C28), while intravesical BCG promotes tumor-supportive TME (C29). However, a recent study shows intra-bladder BCG reprograms HSPCs and enhances APC function (C30).
evaluation: While all claims are supported by citations (Atallah et al., 2024; Daman et al., 2024), the manuscript acknowledges these are contradictory findings requiring further investigation. The authors appropriately note the need to reconcile route-dependent differences, indicating scientific uncertainty in this area.

result: The manuscript describes additional modulators of central trained immunity: MTP-HDL reprograms bone marrow progenitors to suppress tumors and potentiate ICI therapy (C31), obesity-induced changes promote myeloid-biased hematopoiesis and inflammation (C32), and the itaconate pathway regulates trained immunity (C33).
evaluation: All claims are supported by appropriate citations (Priem et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022; Domínguez-Andrés et al., 2019a,b). These represent diverse mechanisms affecting central trained immunity with implications for cancer.

result: The manuscript describes peripheral trained immunity mechanisms. Yeast-derived β-glucan induces trained immunity in pancreatic macrophages/monocytes/neutrophils (C34, C35). Influenza A induces trained immunity in tissue-resident alveolar macrophages that don't originate from circulating monocytes (C36, C37). The peptide DP7 stimulates trained immunity in splenic myeloid cells (C38).
evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by the authors' own work (Geller et al., 2022; Woeste et al., 2023). Claims C36-C37 are supported by Wang et al., 2023, and C38 by Zhang et al., 2025. These represent tissue-specific peripheral trained immunity mechanisms distinct from central training.

result: The manuscript describes additional peripheral trained immunity approaches: CpG-ODN induces metabolic shifts in chicken immune cells (C39), and macrophage membrane-camouflaged BCG targets tumor-associated macrophages (C40).
evaluation: Both claims are supported by citations (Subhasinghe et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). C39 provides cross-species evidence, while C40 represents a targeted delivery approach. Both support the concept of peripheral trained immunity modulation.

result: The manuscript describes trained neutrophil mechanisms: enhanced degranulation and ROS production for tumor killing (C41), type I IFN signaling mediation (C42), cytokine/chemokine release recruiting other immune cells (C43), metabolic shift to glycolysis/Warburg effect (C44), driven by mTOR and HIF1α pathways (C45), and reduction of PMN-MDSCs by oral β-glucan (C46).
evaluation: Claims C41, C44, C45 are supported by citations (Kalafati et al., 2020; Cheng et al., 2014), and C46 by Albeituni et al., 2016. Claims C42 and C43 are stated as established findings but lack direct citations. The mechanisms are consistent with known trained immunity biology.

result: The manuscript describes trained monocyte/macrophage mechanisms: histone modifications (C47), Warburg effect and cytokine production (C48), mitochondrial fission enhancing phagocytosis (C49), M1-like polarization (C50), and ability to penetrate stroma and kill tumor cells, especially with IRE and anti-PD-1 (C51).
evaluation: Claims C47-C48 describe general mechanisms (supported by established knowledge), C49-C50 are supported by citations (Ding et al., 2023; Geller et al., 2022), and C51 is supported by the authors' work (Geller et al., 2022; Woeste et al., 2023). These represent well-characterized trained macrophage functions.

result: The manuscript describes tissue-resident alveolar macrophages acquiring trained immunity after influenza A infection with antitumor functions (C52). Their effects depend on NK cells and IFN-γ but are independent of T cell help, contrasting with adenoviral-induced trained AMs (C53).
evaluation: Both claims are supported by citations (Wang et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2018). The distinction between different viral inducers suggests stimulus-specific trained immunity properties, which is an important mechanistic insight.

result: The manuscript describes trained NK cells and other innate lymphocytes. NK cells trained with cytokines or BCG produce enhanced IFN-γ (C54), influenza A-induced AM training depends on NK cells and IFN-γ (C55), and γδ T cells and innate lymphoid cells acquire trained immunity after vaccination (C56).
evaluation: All claims are supported by appropriate citations (Kleinnijenhuis et al., 2014; Tarannum and Romee, 2021; Wang et al., 2023; Samuel et al., 2024; Taira et al., 2024; Röring et al., 2024). These demonstrate trained immunity extends beyond classical myeloid cells.

result: The manuscript describes links between trained innate immunity and adaptive T cell responses. β-glucan-stimulated DCs show enhanced antigen presentation (C57), CTB stimulates DC training and CD8 T cell responses (C58), combined inducers reduce tumor burden via enhanced DC function (C59), trained macrophages/monocytes upregulate MHC II and costimulatory molecules (C60), trained macrophages secrete CXCL16 attracting T cells (C61), and combining trained immunity with ICI therapy reduces tumor burden (C62).
evaluation: All claims are supported by appropriate citations (Li et al., 2010; Tepale-Segura et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023a; Yao et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023b; Broquet et al., 2024; Geller et al., 2022; Priem et al., 2020; Ylösmäki et al., 2021). These demonstrate important crosstalk between innate and adaptive immunity.

result: Table 1 summarizes preclinical studies of trained immunity inducers across cancer types, including influenza A virus (C63), yeast-derived β-glucan (C64, C66), β-glucan from Trametes versicolor (C65), β-glucan from S. cerevisiae (C67), cholera toxin B (C68), MTP10-HDL (C69), BCG (C70, C71), KK2DP7 (C72), and macrophage membrane-camouflaged BCG (C73).
evaluation: All claims are supported by citations in Table 1 and represent a comprehensive summary of preclinical evidence. The table format appropriately organizes information about cancer types, cell types, stimuli, secondary stimuli, administration routes, and references.

result: The manuscript identifies diverse trained immunity inducers beyond β-glucan and BCG: microbial agents (Hepatitis B virus C74, P. falciparum C75), metabolites (lipoproteins C76, uric acid C77), hormones (aldosterone, catecholamines C78), danger signals (S100-alarmins, heme C79), pathway activators (LXR C80, interferons C81), cytokines (GM-CSF, IL-3 C82), synthetic molecules (Poly I:C C83), metabolic factors (leptin C84), and dietary factors (Western diet C85).
evaluation: All claims are supported by appropriate citations. This comprehensive list demonstrates the breadth of trained immunity inducers, though the manuscript notes their effects in cancer specifically need further investigation. The diversity of inducers is well-established in the literature.

result: The manuscript reports that Knight et al. identified 32 novel small molecule trained immunity inducers through high-throughput screening (C86), with seven validated in vitro and in vivo (C87).
evaluation: Both claims are supported by citation to Knight et al., 2024. This represents a significant expansion of known inducers, though the manuscript appropriately notes their cancer treatment effectiveness requires further determination.

result: The manuscript describes trained immunity approaches in melanoma: ABB i16 β-glucan induces trained immunity in monocytes (C88), CTB enhances DC training (C89), MTP10-HDL improves ICI efficacy (C90), and electrochemotherapy and BCG reshape the TME (C91).
evaluation: All claims are supported by appropriate citations (Vuscan et al., 2024; Priem et al., 2020; Cardillo et al., 2021; Milicevic et al., 2023). These represent diverse therapeutic approaches for melanoma via trained immunity.

result: The manuscript describes trained immunity in lung cancer: yeast-derived β-glucan particles induce sustained responses in lung interstitial macrophages reducing tumors and metastases (C92), and BCG vaccination generates lung-resident memory macrophages (C93).
evaluation: Both claims are supported by citations (Ding et al., 2023; Jeyanathan et al., 2022). These demonstrate tissue-specific trained immunity approaches for lung cancer prevention and treatment.

result: The manuscript describes H. pylori infection inducing trained immunity that heightens monocyte responsiveness via NF-κB signaling, contributing to chronic inflammation and gastric cancer tumorigenesis (C94). H. pylori has dual ability to stimulate and evade immune responses (C95).
evaluation: Both claims are supported by citations (Frauenlob et al., 2023; Dore and Pes, 2024). This represents a tumor-promoting role of trained immunity, contrasting with therapeutic applications.

result: The manuscript describes trained immunity in liver cancer: β-glucan enhances hepatocyte protection via mitophagy and pyroptosis inhibition (C96), BCG promotes apoptosis and immune cell recruitment (C97), SQLE metabolites activate LXR enhancing macrophage immunity (C98), and exercise/infections reprogram Kupffer cells (C99).
evaluation: All claims are supported by appropriate citations (Wang et al., 2024; Vaziri et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Musrati et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2021). These represent diverse mechanisms of trained immunity in liver cancer.

result: The manuscript states that β-glucan enhances peripheral trained immunity in pancreatic cancer, particularly when combined with IRE, resulting in decreased tumor burden and improved survival.
evaluation: This claim is supported by the authors' own work (Geller et al., 2022; Woeste et al., 2023) and represents a key finding for treating immunotherapy-resistant pancreatic cancer.

result: The manuscript describes trained immunity in breast cancer: particulate β-glucan prolongs survival and reduces lung metastases (C101), β-glucan reprograms macrophages to antitumor state (C102), but elevated BMP signaling in bone metastatic niche suppresses this effect (C103). BMP inhibition prior to tumor establishment enhances trained immunity and improves survival (C104).
evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are supported by Ding et al., 2023, and C103-C104 by Ihle et al., 2024. The BMP signaling findings represent an important mechanistic insight into niche-specific regulation of trained immunity.

result: The manuscript describes trained immunity in bladder cancer: modified BCG strains amplify myeloid reprogramming (C105), autophagy is essential for BCG-induced reprogramming (C106), efficacy depends on administration route and strain (C107), intravenous BCG increases CTL infiltration and reduces MDSCs versus intravesical (C108), and β-glucan shows complementary effects (C109).
evaluation: All claims are supported by appropriate citations (Singh et al., 2022; Um et al., 2023; Buffen et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2024; Atallah et al., 2024; Vuscan et al., 2024). These highlight the complexity of BCG therapy optimization.

result: The manuscript describes tumor-promoting effects of trained immunity in liver cancer: hyperlipidemia and DNA hypomethylation drive pro-inflammatory pathways predisposing to HCC (C110), RIPK1 disruption links trained immunity to obesity-associated inflammation (C111), and oxidative stress/inflammasome activation contribute to tumor-promoting microenvironment (C112).
evaluation: All claims are supported by citations (Drummer et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2023; Sohrabi and Reinecke, 2021; Barbier et al., 2019; Dallio et al., 2021). These represent the dual-edged nature of trained immunity.

result: The manuscript describes tumor-promoting trained immunity in lung cancer: macrophage-mediated inflammation creates immunosuppressive niche (C113), and elevated IL-6 supports cancer cell survival and invasion (C114).
evaluation: Both claims are supported by citations (da Costa Loureiro et al., 2020; Snell et al., 2017; Briukhovetska et al., 2021; Rašková et al., 2022). These demonstrate context-dependent effects of trained immunity.

result: The manuscript traces the historical development of BCG cancer therapy: Coley's 1893 observations (C115), Pearl's 1928 tuberculosis-cancer correlation study (C116), Old's mouse model demonstration (C117), establishment of BCG-induced trained immunity (C118-C119), BCG's 1921 development as TB vaccine (C120), Morales' 1976 bladder cancer study (C121), establishment as adjuvant therapy (C122), applications in other cancers (C123), and mediation by trained immunity (C124).
evaluation: All claims are supported by appropriate historical citations. This chronology establishes BCG as the classic example of trained immunity in cancer therapy, though the mechanism was not understood until recently.

result: The manuscript describes β-glucan clinical trials in NSCLC: combination with EGFR-targeting agents and chemotherapy improved ORR (C125), higher anti-β-glucan antibody levels correlated with better survival (C126), combination with VEGF-targeting agents modestly increased ORR (C127), oral WGP reduced MDSCs (C128), and downregulated c-Maf in monocytes (C129).
evaluation: All claims are supported by appropriate clinical trial citations (Thomas et al., 2017; Engel-Riedel et al., 2018; Albeituni et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2020). These represent clinical evidence for β-glucan effects, though benefits are modest.

result: The manuscript describes β-glucan clinical trials in other cancers: lentinan enhanced chemotherapy efficacy in esophageal carcinoma (C130), similar results in breast cancer (C131), high complete response rate with alemtuzumab/rituximab in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (C132), and intravaginal β-glucan improved clearance of cervical lesions (C133).
evaluation: All claims are supported by clinical trial citations (Wang et al., 2012; Ostadrahimi et al., 2024, 2014; Zent et al., 2015; Laccetta et al., 2015). These demonstrate β-glucan effects across multiple cancer types, summarized in Table 2.

result: The manuscript describes β-glucan effects on myelopoiesis in cancer patients: 15-day treatment increased peripheral monocyte counts in breast cancer (C134), white blood cell counts increased in multiple malignancies during chemotherapy (C135), resembling central trained immunity in mice (C136).
evaluation: All claims are supported by citations (Demir et al., 2007; Weitberg, 2008; Mitroulis et al., 2018). These provide clinical evidence for β-glucan-induced myelopoiesis, a hallmark of central trained immunity.

result: The manuscript describes β-glucan effects on quality of life: oral supplements improved energy intake in malnourished cancer patients (C137), and lentinan improved quality of life in gastric/pancreatic cancer patients during chemotherapy (C138).
evaluation: Both claims are supported by citations (Milla et al., 2024; Shimizu et al., 2009; Kataoka et al., 2009). These represent important supportive care benefits beyond direct antitumor effects.

result: The manuscript reports that Moorlag et al. demonstrated chromatin profiling and functional assays can identify individuals in dormant innate immune state, enabling targeted immune-boosting interventions, based on a study of 323 participants with samples at days 0, 14, and 90 post-BCG vaccination.
evaluation: This claim is supported by citation to Moorlag et al., 2024 and represents an important advance in personalized trained immunity approaches. The study design and conclusions are clearly stated.
